title: How to learn world flags without mixing them up

sources.name: Italian Presidency — The Italian Tricolour Flag

practice: Put your eye for detail to the test in World Flags.

sections.html:
A page full of flags can soon become a blur of stripes, stars and familiar colours. Pick five to begin with. Look at each design, cover its name and see which countries you can recall.

You could choose flags from one region or revisit countries you confused in a quiz. A short, familiar set gives you time to notice the details.
sections.title: Start with five flags

sections.html:
Before naming the country, describe what you see:

  • Layout: horizontal stripes, vertical stripes, a cross or a plain background?
  • Colours: which ones appear, and in what order?
  • Symbols: is there a star, emblem or other detail, and where is it?

The edge attached to the flagpole is called the hoist. In a standard illustration with the pole on the left, that is where you start reading vertical stripes. Watch out for photographs showing the flag from the other side.
sections.title: Look at the design in three steps

sections.html:
Italy’s flag has three equal vertical bands: green, white and red, starting at the hoist. Article 12 of the Italian Constitution specifies that design.

“Green by the pole, white in the middle, red at the end” gives you a more useful clue than simply remembering red and green.

Which colour is next to the flagpole?

Green. The order from the hoist is green, white, red.
sections.title: Try it with Italy

sections.html:
If you keep mixing up two flags, compare their labelled illustrations. Look for a difference you can describe: the order of the stripes, an emblem or the position of a star. Then cover the names and try again.

Subtle shades can be unreliable in small images. Screens, lighting and image files affect how colours look. For flags distinguished by precise colours or proportions, check an authoritative reference rather than relying on two thumbnails.
sections.title: Put confusing pairs side by side

sections.html:
After a World Flags round, jot down two or three answers you were unsure about, including lucky guesses. Note the detail that distinguishes each flag.

Before your next round, look at those flags again and try naming them without the labels. Once they feel familiar, add a few more or explore the same countries in World Capitals.
sections.title: Keep a short list for next time

description: Start with a few flags, notice their distinctive details and compare the pairs that keep catching you out.
